The Carmel Pilgrimage

Faithful from the chapels of the Bay Area walk from Monterey to the Basilica of San Carlos Borromeo in Carmel, where Fr. Junípero Serra rests, to lay their petitions at the feet of Our Lady.

Register on Evite

Since 2016 · Organized by St. Aloysius Retreat House

A Pilgrimage of Prayer and Penance

Each October, pilgrims gather at St. Aloysius Retreat House before setting out for Monterey, to begin the walk south to Carmel. What began with twenty-seven pilgrims has continued as a yearly tradition: from El Estero Park, through the streets of Monterey, and on along the coast until the bell towers of the old mission rise above the trees.

Pilgrims arrive footsore and singing, to kneel where Fr. Serra himself once knelt, and to entrust the intentions of their families, their parishes, and the whole Church to the Mother of God.

Join us on this pilgrimage and offer the day for your own special intentions, or for the intentions of our faithful.

“We go up on foot, as pilgrims always have, because some graces are only granted to those willing to walk for them.”
— A pilgrim

The Way South

8:00 AM — Meet in Los Gatos for mass

Pilgrims gather at St. Aloysius Retreat House. Donuts, coffee, and juice are served in the lower courtyard.

9:30 AM — Depart for Monterey

Cars leave Los Gatos together for the coast.

11:00 AM — Arrive at El Estero Park

971 Pearl Street, Monterey. Restrooms available; please bring your own lunch. Fr. Asher and Fr. Caley lead the pilgrims in prayer before setting out.

12:00 PM — The pilgrimage begins

On foot from Dennis the Menace Park, the Rosary begins as the pilgrims walk on through the streets of Monterey and into Carmel.

5:00 PM — Arrival at the Basilica

The pilgrims arrive at Mission San Carlos Borroméo (Carmel Mission) for a final prayer at the tomb of Fr. Serra.

5:45 PM — Pizza

Pizza is provided at the mission to close a day eight miles in the making.

What Pilgrims Carry Home

By mile ten my feet had stopped complaining and my heart had started praying properly. That is the whole secret of the thing.— Thomas, pilgrim since 2019
I brought my two boys the year they turned twelve. We still talk about the Mass on the beach more than anything else that year.— A mother from San Jose
You walk alone with your thoughts for a while, then someone starts a decade of the Rosary, and you remember why you came.— Margaret, first-time pilgrim, 2022
